feedback: If a learner says cancer is caught or invades from outside, redirect to the mechanism: these are the body's own cells dividing because their control genes have failed (some infections, such as HPV, can raise the risk of certain cancers, but you cannot catch cancer cells from another person).

If a learner assumes one mutation causes cancer, point out that many mutations have no effect (for example, they fall outside genes or are silent because of the genetic code's redundancy), that mutations elsewhere in a gene do not necessarily cause cancer, and that cancer usually requires several specific control-gene mutations.
If a learner treats cancer as a single disease with one cause, highlight that it is many diseases arising from different accumulated control failures.
activities.intendedInsight: Cancer is loss of cell-cycle control from accumulated DNA mutations disabling tumour-suppressor genes or activating oncogenes, so mitosis runs unchecked — it is the body's own cells, and it is many diseases arising from control failure rather than one catchable disease.
learnerActions: Trace a cell-cycle diagram and identify the control checkpoints that normally decide whether a cell divides.

Predict what happens as mutations build up that disable tumour-suppressor genes or activate oncogenes, then observe or reason through (in a simplified model) division becoming unchecked and a tumour forming once enough control failures have accumulated.

Follow the sequence: normal cell → control genes disabled → uncontrolled division → tumour, stating in your own words why cancer is the body's OWN cells rather than an external invader (even though some infections, such as HPV, can raise the risk of certain cancers, the tumour cells themselves are the body's own).
State explicitly that cancer typically requires several specific mutations in control genes, not a single event.
activities.title: Build the mechanism: cell cycle, checkpoints and runaway division

feedback: If a learner says any stem cell can become anything, distinguish potency levels and the role of the source (embryonic vs adult vs iPS).
If a learner treats stem cells as a guaranteed cure-all, acknowledge the medical promise while separating it from current, source-dependent limits.
If a learner conflates a stem cell with a cancer cell because both divide a lot, contrast a stem cell's regulated capacity to differentiate with a cancer cell's unregulated division.
activities.intendedInsight: Stem cells are unspecialised, self-renewing cells able to differentiate, unlike fixed-function specialised cells; their source and potency (embryonic vs adult/tissue vs iPS) differ, and this scientific accuracy is needed before the ethics.
learnerActions: Use a differentiation tree to follow one unspecialised stem cell branching into different specialised cell types.
In a differentiation sandbox, choose lineages and turn a single stem cell into different specialised types, noting that a specialised cell has a fixed function.
Complete a comparison table of embryonic vs adult/tissue vs induced pluripotent (iPS) stem cells across potency, source, and ethical considerations.
Explain in your own words why stem cells are medically valuable for regenerative medicine, and why not every stem cell can become anything.
activities.title: Stem cells vs specialised cells: sources, potency and differentiation

feedback: If a learner claims iPS/adult cells remove the ethical issue completely, prompt them to consider which objections they address and which remain.
If a learner collapses the debate into pure fact or pure opinion, ask them to sort specific questions into empirical versus value categories.
If a learner treats genetic testing as settled by the test result alone, ask which questions the result answers and which value questions (who sees it, what action follows, consent) remain open.
Establish a safe, respectful classroom before this discussion; a lower-stakes analogue such as IVF can be used first to practise the format.
activities.intendedInsight: Structured socioscientific methods let learners weigh multiple stakeholders' perspectives and locate genuine disagreement in differing values, not in ignorance, while keeping empirical and ethical questions distinct — and the same approach transfers from embryonic-stem-cell research to genetic testing.
learnerActions: In a structured group discussion, take on a stakeholder role (e.g. prospective patient, researcher, ethicist) — for example reviewing a clinical-trial application.
Build an ethical matrix mapping stakeholders against principles to weigh different perspectives systematically.
Consider whether adult and iPS cells, which can be used without embryos, dissolve the ethical objection entirely or only part of it, and explain why.

Apply the same structured approach (ethical matrix, empirical-vs-value sorting) to genetic testing as a second socioscientific issue in this topic, identifying its distinct stakeholders and value tensions (e.g. privacy, consent, what to do with predictive results), and articulating at least two arguments for and at least two against, each in its strongest form.
Separate the empirical questions evidence can settle from the value questions it cannot, and record where reasonable, informed people could still disagree because they weigh values differently.
activities.title: Structured discussion: role-play, ethical matrix, and genetic testing
